A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Spatial-DISE, with the same research identity, core benchmark and generation framework. Their main text, tables, figures, equations and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLM evaluations, supervised fine-tuning experiments, a 54-participant human assessment and analysis of 200 model errors.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds model evaluations, external benchmark results, quadrant-transfer experiments and a layout ablation.

M1.justification: The DISE framework, ten task designs, five Blender generation algorithms in Appendix A.4 and LoRA fine-tuning approach are retained. The added quadrant and layout experiments evaluate existing components. Expanded verification documentation does not establish a changed generation algorithm or model.

E1.justification: External fine-tuning evaluation expands from CVBench, SAT_test and SPACE in v1 to also include OmniSpatial and VSIBench_MCQ in v3 Table 3. The 559-item Spatial-DISE benchmark, ten core tasks and 12,355-item collection remain. This extends external dataset coverage within the existing spatial-reasoning scope.

E2.justification: v3 adds GPT-5, o4-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash with and without thinking to the reported Spatial-DISE comparisons, increasing evaluated models from 28 to 32. Tables 2 and the appendix task-results table retain the earlier models; human and random baselines also remain.

E3.justification: The reported SFT budget changes from three epochs in v1 Table 13 to two in v3 Table 14. New evaluation designs train on individual DISE quadrants and test across quadrants and 2D tasks, while Section 5.2 compares merged versus separate image inputs. These substantially extend the experimental design. Human matrix sampling and CTT/IRT analysis already appeared in v1 Appendix B.1.

E4.justification: v3 Figure 3 adds quadrant-specific training analyses testing cross-quadrant specialization and asymmetric 3D-to-2D transfer. Section 5.2 adds a layout ablation testing whether multi-panel image parsing explains failures. These materially extend validation beyond the retained full-dataset fine-tuning and 200-error analysis.

E5.justification: v1 Table 3 reports 95% confidence intervals for base accuracy, SFT accuracy and their differences; v3 replaces these with point estimates and differences without intervals. Table 2 confidence intervals and Appendix B.1's CTT/IRT uncertainty procedures remain. No increased repeated-run count is documented.

E6.justification: Under the revised training budget, Tables 2–3 replace Qwen-SFT's 49.7% and SpaceOm-SFT's 33.8% with 47.0% and 41.3%. SpaceOm's reported CVBench fine-tuning outcome changes from 68.8% to 36.4% in v1 to 68.8% to 70.33% in v3, reversing the forgetting finding. New model, benchmark and ablation results are added. However, v3 Appendix Table 13 retains SpaceOm-SFT at 33.8%, contradicting its main tables.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 retains the same CTT and two-parameter logistic IRT equations, variance calculations and confidence-interval formulas. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation appears. The expanded taxonomy discussion is conceptual interpretation.

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the taxonomy's novelty claim: v1's 'A Novel and Unified Taxonomy' and 'introduce' become 'A Cognitively Grounded Taxonomy' and 'adopt' in v3. The central contributions of a benchmark, scalable generation pipeline and diagnosis of a substantial human–VLM gap remain.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes fragile generalization and catastrophic forgetting; v3 argues for selective external generalization without forgetting and interprets transfer patterns as quadrant specialization. Appendix A.1 newly distinguishes task structure from the cognitive strategies used to solve it. Section 6 adds concrete limitations concerning LLM-judge bias, the 200-error sample, sim-to-real transfer and incomplete manual verification.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies batch size 48, warmup ratio 0.05 and DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, and adds API identifiers for the new models. It narrows manual-verification documentation to benchmark review and a stratified 1,000-item sample with programmatic checks for the remaining training collection. The abstract changes a promised resource release to stated availability through a project link; availability was not externally verified.

R1.justification: v3 reframes the taxonomy as adopted from cognitive science and adds an argument that aggregating existing benchmarks would retain imbalance, heterogeneous formats and insufficient verifiable training data. Table 1 changes SAT's intrinsic-dynamic coverage from present to absent. Montello (2005) and Tversky (2005) background references are removed; most related work remains.

P1.justification: Rewriting is concentrated in Section 4.3, now organized around four research questions, and the conclusion/limitations section. Error analysis gains subsections, manuscript statements move before the references, and 'wild data' becomes 'real-world data'. Author affiliations and publication headers change, while much of the introduction, methodology and appendix prose remains.

P2.justification: v3 substantially restructures Table 3, adds two transfer heatmaps and a layout-ablation table, restyles Figures 1–2 and expands model-result tables. The generation diagram moves from v1 Figure 3 to Appendix Figure 4; the rule-application example moves from the main text to Appendix Figure 12 and is enlarged. These are substantial display changes; the underlying error examples are retained.

improvement.justification: The new transfer and layout controls, broader external evaluation and more explicit limitations strengthen validation and interpretation. However, v3 removes cross-benchmark confidence intervals and leaves central SFT results inconsistent: SpaceOm-SFT is 41.3% in Tables 2–3 but 33.8% in Appendix Table 13. The forgetting conclusion also reverses under changed training settings. These reporting problems leave the reliability of the expanded generalization evidence unclear, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
